7460:
"Head over heels" most commonly means being so deeply and completely in love with someone that you feel overwhelmed, dizzy, and out of control — like you've lost your footing and are tumbling through the air. It describes love at its most intense and all-consuming.

Think of it this way: when you fall so hard for someone that your whole world feels like it's spinning, that's being head over heels in love.

Examples:

  • "She fell head over heels in love with him the moment they met."
  • "He is head over heels for her — he can't stop thinking about her."
  • "I was head over heels in love before I even knew her name."

This idiom doesn't just mean "I really like this person." It means something much stronger. It describes the kind of love that:

  • hits you suddenly and completely
  • makes you feel dizzy, off-balance, almost out of control
  • takes over your thoughts and emotions
  • makes rational thinking difficult

If someone says they are "a little in love," that's mild. If they say they are head over heels, that's total, overwhelming, can't-eat-can't-sleep love. The intensity is the point.
The Origin — Where Did This Phrase Come From?

This is where it gets fascinating. The original phrase was actually the opposite — "heels over head."

Imagine doing a somersault or a cartwheel. Your heels literally go over your head. That's a real physical event — it describes being turned completely upside down, flipped, tumbling. The phrase "heels over head" made perfect logical sense and was used as far back as the 14th century in English. Some scholars trace versions of it even to ancient Latin texts.

Over time, through common usage, people began saying it the other way around — "head over heels" — which is actually the normal, everyday position of a human body (your head is always over your heels when you're standing). So ironically, the phrase got flipped, even though the flipped version makes less literal sense. But language doesn't always follow logic — it follows people, and people said "head over heels" enough that it became the accepted standard form by around the early 19th century.

The key image, however, remained the same: tumbling, flipping, being upside down and off-balance. That sensation of spinning out of control is what the phrase is designed to capture.
Why a Tumbling Image for Love?

This is a beautiful piece of linguistic thinking. Love — especially new, overwhelming love — feels physically destabilizing. You feel:

  • dizzy (butterflies, lightheadedness)
  • off-balance (you can't concentrate, you're distracted)
  • out of control (you didn't choose to feel this way — it just happened)
  • like you're falling (note: we also say "falling in love," for the same reason)

The image of a person tumbling head over heels — spinning through the air, upside down, with no grip on the ground — perfectly mirrors these emotional sensations. The idiom is a metaphor that maps a physical experience onto an emotional one.
Can It Be Used for Things Other Than Romantic Love?

Yes, though less commonly. "Head over heels" can sometimes describe extreme enthusiasm or excitement about something beyond romance.

Examples:

  • "She is head over heels about her new job."
  • "The kids were head over heels excited about the trip to Disney World."

However, be aware that when used this way, it can sound slightly informal or exaggerated. The romantic meaning is by far the most common and widely understood usage. If you use it in a non-romantic context, people will understand you, but they may find it a slightly unusual choice of words.

The idiom shows up in a few reliable patterns. Here are the ones you'll encounter most:

1. Fall head over heels (in love)
This is the most classic form. The verb "fall" reinforces the idea of tumbling and losing control.
"I fell head over heels in love with Paris the first time I visited."

2. Be head over heels (in love)
Describes a current, ongoing state of deep love.
"She is head over heels in love with her partner."

3. Head over heels for someone
"He is completely head over heels for her."

4. Head over heels about something
Used for the non-romantic sense.
"She's head over heels about her new apartment."

It's worth being clear about what this idiom does not mean, to avoid confusion:

  • It does not mean someone is literally doing somersaults or cartwheels (unless you're being humorous or very literal in a playful context).
  • It does not suggest something negative about love — it's almost always used positively or affectionately, even if the love is described as overwhelming.
  • It does not mean a mild or casual liking. It always implies intensity and depth.

"Head over heels" is an informal, conversational expression. You'd use it in:

  • Everyday speech
  • Casual writing
  • Novels, songs, and poetry
  • Friendly conversation

You would not typically use it in formal writing, legal documents, academic papers, or professional business emails. It belongs to the warm, human, emotional side of language.

If you want to always remember what this idiom means, just picture this:

A person is so in love that they literally lose their footing and start tumbling — head over heels, spinning through the air, completely upside down and out of control.

That image of joyful, chaotic, helpless tumbling is what head over heels love feels like. Once you see that picture, the meaning will never leave you.

"Head over heels" means to be completely, overwhelmingly, and deeply in love (or occasionally, very excited about something) — so much so that you feel dizzy and out of control, like you're tumbling upside down through the air.
7461:
A head start is an advantage you have at the very beginning of something — before others get going, or compared to where others are starting from.

Think of it this way: imagine a foot race. Everyone is lined up at the starting line. But you are allowed to begin 20 metres ahead of everyone else. When the race starts, you already have a lead — not because you ran faster, but simply because you began from a better position. That 20-metre advantage is your head start.

The word captures two things at once:

  • You are ahead (in front).
  • It is at the start (the beginning).

A head start means something is already working in your favour before the effort even begins. This advantage can take many forms:

  • Time — You began earlier than others, so you have had more time to work, learn, or prepare.
  • Knowledge or skill — You already know something or can do something that others are still learning.
  • Resources — You already have money, tools, connections, or support that others don't have yet.
  • Position — You are literally or figuratively further along than others from the very beginning.

In all cases, the key is that the advantage exists at the start, not something you earned in the middle or at the end.

In its most literal sense, a head start is used in physical races or competitions where one person or team is allowed to begin ahead of others.

For example:

  • In a running race, a younger child might be given a head start of 10 metres so the race is fairer against an older, faster competitor.
  • In a car race, one driver might start at the front of the grid while others start behind.
  • In a board game like a quiz, one team might get a head start of 5 points before the game begins.

Here, the head start is a concrete, measurable gap — you can physically see it.

This is where the word is used most often. In everyday conversation, a head start refers to any advantage a person has at the beginning of a challenge, goal, journey, or competition in life — even when there is no actual race happening.

Here are some common examples:

  • A child who learns to read at age 3 has a head start in school compared to children who learn at age 6.
  • If you save money from a young age, you get a head start on building wealth.
  • A job applicant who already knows the company's CEO has a head start over other applicants in getting hired.
  • If you start studying for an exam two weeks early instead of the night before, you give yourself a head start.
  • A person born into a wealthy family has a head start in life compared to someone born into poverty.

In all of these, no actual race is happening. The word is simply describing the idea that one person begins in a better position than others due to some pre-existing advantage.
Common Phrases and How the Word Is Used

The noun "head start" is used in a few very natural patterns. Here are the ones you will encounter most often:

1. "Get a head start"
This means you act early or take steps in advance so that you are ahead of others or ahead of schedule.

  • "I want to get a head start on my homework before the weekend."
  • "Let's leave an hour early to get a head start on the traffic."

2. "Have a head start"
This describes already being in a position of advantage — usually because of something that already happened or something you already possess.

  • "She has a head start because she studied this topic last year."
  • "He has a head start over other candidates because he already speaks three languages."

3. "Give someone a head start"
This means you deliberately allow someone else to begin earlier or from a better position — often to be fair, or to be kind, or to help them.

  • "The coach gave the younger players a head start in the drill."
  • "His parents gave him a head start by paying for his university education."
An Important Nuance: A Head Start Does NOT Guarantee Success

This is a subtle but very important point. A head start gives you an advantage at the beginning — but it does not mean you will definitely win or succeed in the end. It simply means you started in a better position.

  • The child who learned to read at age 3 might still struggle in school later.
  • The person who saved money early might make poor investments.
  • The job applicant who knew the CEO might still perform badly in the interview.

A head start improves your chances and reduces the effort needed — but it is only a starting advantage, not a guaranteed outcome. This is why we often say someone "squandered their head start" (wasted it) or "made the most of their head start" (used it well).
How Big Can a Head Start Be?

A head start can be small or large. You can describe its size naturally:

  • "She had a slight head start." (a small advantage)
  • "He had a significant head start." (a big advantage)
  • "They had a massive head start over their competitors." (a huge advantage)

The bigger the head start, the more difficult it is for others to catch up.

A head start is an advantage — in time, knowledge, skill, position, or resources — that a person or group has at the very beginning of something, placing them ahead of others before the real effort has even begun.
7462: At the heart of "head-on" is a single, powerful idea: directness. When something happens head-on, it happens in the most direct, straight-forward way possible — with no angle, no detour, and no avoidance. Picture two cars driving toward each other on the same road: their fronts meet each other directly. That image is the soul of this word.

1. The Literal Meaning — A Direct Physical Collision or Contact

In its literal sense, "head-on" describes how two things physically meet or collide — directly from the front, not from the side or at an angle.

  • The two trains collided head-on. — The front of one train smashed into the front of the other, straight on.
  • The hurricane struck the island head-on. — It hit the island directly, not at a glancing angle.
  • The ball flew head-on into the wall. — It traveled in a straight line and hit the wall directly at the front.

The defining detail here is always the same: front meets front, with no sideways or angled movement. A crash from the side is not head-on. A collision at an angle is not head-on. Only a direct, frontal meeting is.

2. The Figurative Meaning — Confronting Something Directly and Boldly

This is the meaning you will encounter most often in everyday life. When a person does something head-on, they face it directly, without avoiding or dancing around it. They don't delay, soften the blow, or try to sneak around the difficulty — they go straight at it.

  • She tackled the problem head-on. — She didn't ignore the problem or look for a workaround. She dealt with it directly.
  • He confronted his boss head-on about the unfair pay. — He didn't hint at it, drop subtle clues, or complain to others behind closed doors. He spoke directly and clearly to his boss.
  • The government chose to address the crisis head-on. — Rather than avoiding the hard decisions, they dealt with the crisis directly.
  • She faced her fear of public speaking head-on. — She didn't hide from it. She went straight into the uncomfortable thing and confronted it.
The Tone and Feeling it Carries

In the figurative sense, "head-on" quietly signals courage and decisiveness. When you say someone handled something head-on, you are suggesting they were bold — they chose the harder, more direct path instead of avoiding the issue. It is generally said with admiration, or at least neutral respect.

That said, depending on the context, it can occasionally carry a hint of recklessness — the idea that someone charged straight into a situation without much subtlety or caution, like a bull running head-on into a wall. But this negative shade is far less common. In most uses, head-on is a compliment in disguise.

Understanding a word also means knowing what it is not. The opposite of head-on is anything that avoids, delays, or approaches indirectly:

Sidestepping an issue, tiptoeing around a problem, talking about something in circles, hitting something at an angle, or choosing to ignore a challenge — all of these are the opposite of head-on. If someone "beats around the bush," they are doing the exact opposite of addressing something head-on.

As an adverb, "head-on" always follows a verb and tells you how the action was done. Here are the verbs it most naturally pairs with:

face something head-on, tackle something head-on, confront something head-on, address something head-on, deal with something head-on, meet something head-on, collide head-on, hit something head-on.

You will almost always see it at or near the end of a sentence or clause.

This is easy in practice. Ask yourself: is the sentence about physical objects (vehicles, storms, projectiles)? Then it's likely literal. Is it about problems, emotions, conflicts, or challenges? Then it's almost certainly figurative. The grammar is the same; only the context changes the meaning.
A Quick Summary to Lock it In

"Head-on" as an adverb means: directly, from the front, without avoiding or going around. It describes either a straight-on physical collision between two things, or the bold, direct way a person faces a problem or challenge. Either way, the spirit of the word is always the same — no detour, no evasion, straight at it.
7463:
A headbutt is a forceful strike delivered using the head — specifically the forehead (the hard, bony front part of your skull) — as the weapon. It is the act of driving your head into someone or something with force and intent.

Think of it this way: just as a punch uses a fist, and a kick uses a foot, a headbutt uses the head. The head becomes both the tool and the weapon.

When a headbutt occurs, a person thrusts their head forward sharply and powerfully, making contact — usually forehead to forehead, or forehead to face/body — with a target. The impact is sudden, hard, and concentrated. Because the human skull is one of the strongest bones in the body, it can deliver a very powerful blow, often causing pain, injury, or even unconsciousness to the person on the receiving end.

• The striking part: The forehead is the primary point of contact — the flat, hard area just above your eyebrows. This is the thickest and most solid part of the skull, which is why it is used rather than, say, the top or side of the head.
  • The target: A headbutt is most commonly aimed at another person's face, nose, or forehead, though it can also be directed at any part of the body, or even an object.
  • The motion: The motion is a sharp, forward thrust — like a ram charging. It is short, explosive, and direct. There is no swinging involved, unlike a punch. The power comes from the neck, shoulders, and core driving the skull forward.

1. In fighting and violence
This is the most common context. A headbutt is an aggressive act used in street fights or brawls. It is often a surprise move because people typically expect punches and kicks, not a strike from the head. It can be devastating because it catches people off guard and uses a part of the body they don't usually "see coming."

Example: During the argument, he suddenly delivered a headbutt that knocked his opponent to the ground.

2. In sports
In many professional combat sports (such as boxing and MMA), a headbutt is an illegal move — it is banned because it is considered too dangerous and unsportsmanlike. When it happens accidentally during a match, a referee may stop the fight and assess the damage. In football (soccer), headbutts occasionally happen and are met with red cards and serious disciplinary action.

The most famous sporting headbutt in history is arguably the one delivered by French footballer Zinedine Zidane to Italian player Marco Materazzi in the 2006 FIFA World Cup Final — it became a global talking point precisely because headbutts are so unusual and shocking in that setting.

3. In the animal world
Many animals naturally headbutt as part of their behaviour — particularly as a way of fighting, establishing dominance, or defending territory. Goats, rams (male sheep), and bulls are classic examples. When two rams collide skull-to-skull at high speed to compete for dominance, that collision is a headbutt.

Example: The two rams charged at each other and exchanged powerful headbutts.

4. Playful or affectionate use
Interestingly, the word can also be used in a soft, informal, even affectionate sense. Cats, for example, are well known for pressing or bumping their heads gently against humans or other cats as a sign of affection and trust. This gentle action is often called a headbutt in everyday speech, even though it has nothing aggressive about it.

Example: My cat came over and gave me a little headbutt on my chin.

Here, the word is used loosely and warmly — the "force" is minimal, and the meaning is almost the opposite of the violent version. Context always tells you which kind is meant.

As a noun, "headbutt" refers to a single instance of this action — one complete strike.

  • He threw a headbutt. (He performed the action.)
  • It was a vicious headbutt. (Describing the strike itself.)
  • The headbutt ended the fight immediately. (Referring to that one act.)

You can also say "a headbutt to the nose" or "a headbutt to the chest" to specify where the strike landed.

To bring it all together: a headbutt is the act of using your head — particularly the hard forehead — as a striking tool to hit someone or something with force. It lives most naturally in the world of combat, violence, and aggressive sports, but it also appears in nature (animals) and even in gentle, affectionate behaviour (cats). The common thread across all uses is the same physical action: head meets target, with intent and contact. What changes is only the force and the feeling behind it.
7464:
When you do something headfirst, your head leads — it goes before the rest of your body. That is the root image locked inside this word.

Think of a swimmer diving into a pool: the head enters the water first, then the shoulders, then the rest of the body. That is headfirst in its purest, most physical sense.

Headfirst is used in two ways — one literal, one figurative — and both grow from the same root image.

Meaning 1 — Literal (Physical Movement)

When a person or thing moves so that the head leads the body, they are moving headfirst.

She fell headfirst down the staircase.
He slid headfirst into the muddy ditch.
The child tumbled headfirst off the bicycle.

Here, headfirst is purely describing the direction and position of the body during movement. The head is in front. The rest follows.

Notice that this movement often happens suddenly — a fall, a dive, a slide. It rarely describes slow, controlled, everyday walking. There is almost always some kind of momentum or force involved.

Meaning 2 — Figurative (Rushing Into Something Without Caution)

This is where the word gets much more interesting, and it is also the more common way headfirst is used in everyday language.

When you do something headfirst in a figurative sense, you throw yourself into it quickly, eagerly, and often without fully thinking it through first. You don't pause. You don't prepare carefully. You just go — head first, before the rest of you has had time to catch up.

He jumped headfirst into the new business without doing any research.
She dived headfirst into the relationship, ignoring all the warning signs.
After watching one video about cooking, he plunged headfirst into opening a restaurant.

The core feeling here is: fast, impulsive, with full commitment but limited caution.
The Tone — Is It Good or Bad?

This is important: headfirst is not purely negative, but it always carries a slight warning underneath it.

The word suggests two things at once:

  • Enthusiasm and boldness — you went in fully, without holding back
  • A lack of careful preparation — you didn't think it all through before jumping

Whether that comes across as brave or reckless depends entirely on the context and the outcome.

If someone dives headfirst into a new career and succeeds, it sounds bold and admirable. If someone dives headfirst into a bad investment and loses everything, it sounds impulsive and foolish. The word itself doesn't judge — but it always hints that the person didn't proceed with caution.

Think of it this way: the opposite of headfirst (in the figurative sense) would be someone who researches thoroughly, plans carefully, tests the water slowly, and then proceeds step by step. That person is the opposite of headfirst.
The Verbs That Pair With It

Headfirst almost always follows action verbs that describe entering or moving into something. The most common combinations are:

  • Dive headfirst — the most natural and frequent pairing
  • Jump headfirst
  • Plunge headfirst
  • Rush headfirst
  • Throw oneself headfirst
  • Fall headfirst

You will notice that these are all verbs of forward, committed movement. That is not a coincidence — headfirst intensifies them by adding the image of full-body commitment where even your head, your most precious and vulnerable part, goes first.
How to Recognise It in a Sentence

Ask yourself two questions:

  1. Is someone moving or entering something, either physically or in terms of a life situation?
  2. Is there a sense of speed, eagerness, or lack of careful thought?

If yes to both, headfirst is doing its work.

"He dived headfirst into the argument."

Here, no one is actually diving. But he entered the argument fast, fully, and probably without thinking it through — exactly the way a body enters water headfirst.
A Final Image to Lock It In

Imagine two people standing at the edge of a pool.

Person A walks to the steps, slowly lowers one foot, tests the temperature, thinks about it, and carefully gets in.

Person B takes a few steps back, runs, and dives — head going in first, fully committed, no hesitation, no testing.

Person B is acting headfirst — in every sense of the word.
7465: The word heading has several distinct meanings depending on the context. All of them share a common thread: something that tops, leads, or points forward. Here is every important meaning explained fully.
1. A title or label at the top of written content

This is the most common meaning in everyday life. A heading is a short piece of text placed at the top of a page, section, chapter, document, email, or any block of content. Its purpose is to tell you — before you read — what the content below is about. Think of it as a signpost.

A heading is always meant to be brief and informative. It prepares the reader for what follows.

Examples:

  • A newspaper article has a heading (the bold line at the top — what people commonly call a headline) that tells you what the story is about.
  • A book chapter might have the heading "Chapter 4: The Journey Begins."
  • A long report might have multiple headings like "Introduction," "Findings," and "Conclusion" to divide it into clear sections.
  • A form might have headings like "Personal Details" or "Payment Information" to group related fields together.
  • An official letter often begins with a heading that states the sender's address and the date.

When a document has smaller titles beneath the main heading, those are called subheadings. For example, a chapter called "Health" might have subheadings like "Diet," "Exercise," and "Sleep" within it. Subheadings break a large section into smaller, more navigable parts.

In digital writing — word processors like Microsoft Word, Google Docs, or web pages — headings are a formal structural feature. In HTML (the language of websites), headings are tagged as H1, H2, H3, and so on, where H1 is the most important (usually the page title), H2 is a section title, H3 is a subsection title, and so forth. This hierarchy helps both readers and search engines understand the structure of the content.

In a legal or official document, the heading of a section is the short descriptive label that identifies what that section covers. Courts and lawmakers use it to summarize a clause before its full text.

In navigation — whether by sea or air — a heading is the direction a vehicle is pointing, expressed as a compass bearing measured in degrees.

Imagine a full circle with 360 degrees. North is 0° (or 360°), East is 90°, South is 180°, and West is 270°. Every direction between these can be expressed as a number in degrees.

Examples:

  • "The captain ordered a heading of 270 degrees" — meaning the ship is now pointing due west.
  • "Maintain your current heading" — the pilot should keep flying in the same direction.
  • "We changed our heading to avoid the storm."

An important distinction — heading vs. course:
A heading is where the vehicle is pointed. But because of wind (for aircraft) or ocean currents (for ships), the vehicle may not actually travel in the exact direction it is pointing. The actual path the vehicle traces over the ground is called the course (or track). For example, a plane pointed east (heading: 090°) may be drifted slightly southeast by strong crosswinds, so its actual course over the ground is 110°. Pilots and navigators must account for this difference.

In casual, everyday language, people also use "heading" loosely to mean general direction — "We were on a heading toward the mountains" — even when no precise degrees are involved.
3. A tunnel driven into rock (mining and civil engineering)

In mining and tunneling, a heading is a horizontal tunnel or passage that is dug forward into the rock face or earth.

It is typically a narrow, preliminary tunnel cut into the mine to explore, access, or prepare an area for larger excavation. Miners drive a heading — meaning they progressively dig it forward, advancing its length over time.

Examples:

  • "The miners advanced the heading by fifteen meters this week."
  • "A new heading was opened to reach the coal seam."
  • "The heading collapsed before they could shore it up."

The word is used this way because the tunnel is literally "heading into" the rock — pushing forward into uncharted material.
4. The top section of a curtain (interior design and soft furnishing)

In curtain-making and home furnishing, the heading is the top part of a curtain — the section at the very top where the fabric is gathered, folded, or pleated so it can be attached to a curtain rod, track, or rail.

The heading determines both the visual style of the curtain (how it hangs and drapes) and how much fabric is needed to make it. Different heading styles are named and widely recognized in this field:

  • Pencil pleat heading — The fabric at the top is gathered into tight, narrow, cylindrical pleats that look like a row of pencils standing side by side. This is the most traditional style.
  • Eyelet heading — Large metal rings (eyelets) are punched through the top of the fabric at regular intervals, and the curtain rod passes directly through these rings. This gives a modern, casual look.
  • Tab top heading — Loops of fabric (tabs) are sewn at the top, and the rod threads through them.
  • Pinch pleat heading — The fabric is pinched into deep, formal pleats at regular intervals and stitched in place. This is a classic, tailored look.
  • Wave heading — The fabric flows in soft, even, uniform waves. Often used in contemporary interiors.

Examples:

  • "She chose an eyelet heading for the bedroom curtains because it looked more relaxed."
  • "The heading needs to be at least 15 cm deep for the pleats to form properly."
  • "When buying fabric for curtains with a pencil pleat heading, you typically need two to two-and-a-half times the width of the window."
5. The act of hitting a ball with the head (football/soccer) — less common

In British English, particularly in football (soccer), a heading can refer to the act of deliberately striking the ball with one's head to pass it, control it, or score. However, this usage is less common as a noun — the word header is far more frequently used in this sense today.

  • More common: "He scored with a brilliant header."
  • Less common but valid: "His heading of the ball into the net was perfectly timed."

You might encounter this in older writing or formal match reports.

Every sense of the word "heading" shares an underlying idea: something that is at the top, at the front, or points forward.

  • A document heading sits at the top of the content.
  • A navigation heading points the vehicle forward in a direction.
  • A mining heading pushes forward into rock.
  • A curtain heading is at the top of the curtain.
  • A football heading uses the top of the body (the head) to play the ball.

Once you see this, the word becomes easy to understand in any context — whatever is leading or topping something is its heading.
7466: "Headlong" describes something — most often a movement, action, or process — happening with great speed, uncontrolled force, and a complete absence of caution. It is the opposite of slow and careful. Something headlong charges forward without pausing, without thinking, and without brakes.

1. The literal meaning — moving with the head going first

In its physical, real-world sense, "headlong" describes moving or falling with the head leading the way forward. Imagine a person tripping on a step and crashing forward, head first — that is a headlong fall. Imagine someone diving off a ledge, body tilted so the head cuts through the air before anything else — that is a headlong dive.

2. The figurative meaning — recklessly fast and uncontrolled

This is by far the more common and important use of the word. Here, "headlong" doesn't literally mean head-first. It describes something done with such reckless, uncontrolled urgency that it feels like a forward plunge — no pause, no braking, no careful calculation. It's the quality of hurling yourself into something without looking where you're going.

This is where the word gets its power and its personality.

Picture a boulder rolling down a steep hill. It doesn't slow down. It doesn't weigh its options. The momentum just takes it — fast, forward, and unstoppably. That is the energy trapped inside the word "headlong."

Now picture a person who, after one terrible day at work, quits their job, abandons their apartment, and moves to another city — all within a week, without a plan. That is a headlong escape from their old life.

The speed is always there. But what truly defines "headlong" is the loss of control — the sense that something is being driven forward by pure force or impulse, not by careful thought.

• Speed — It is always fast. Slow and headlong cannot coexist.
  • Recklessness — There is little or no regard for dangers, consequences, or what lies ahead.
  • Uncontrolled momentum — Once something headlong starts, it seems either unwilling or unable to stop.
  • Forward drive — It always moves toward something, even if blindly. It is never passive.
Common Phrases Where You'll Encounter It

• A headlong rush — charging into something fast and carelessly
  • A headlong plunge — diving into something without control (physical or figurative)
  • A headlong fall — tumbling forward, head-first and uncontrolled
  • A headlong dash — sprinting with wild, uncontrolled urgency
  • A headlong pursuit — chasing something with reckless, unstoppable intensity
Sentences That Show It in Action

1. The country's headlong rush into war alarmed its allies. — The country moved toward war so fast and carelessly, with no time taken to think, that those watching were alarmed.
  2. She made a headlong dive to catch the ball before it hit the ground. — She threw herself forward, head first, without hesitation.
  3. His headlong pursuit of wealth cost him his health and his family. — He chased money with such reckless, unstoppable obsession that he destroyed what truly mattered.
  4. The startled horses broke into a headlong gallop across the field. — Frightened, the horses ran at full, uncontrolled speed.
  5. The company's headlong expansion into new markets ended in disaster. — The company grew too fast, too recklessly, without enough thought — and paid the price.

Many words describe carelessness or speed, but "headlong" is stronger and more specific than all of them.

  • Hasty means doing something quickly without enough preparation. It's relatively mild — a hasty decision is simply rushed. A headlong decision carries the sense of throwing yourself into it with physical force.
  • Reckless means without care for danger or consequences. But reckless doesn't imply momentum or speed the way "headlong" does. You can be reckless while standing still. You cannot be headlong while standing still.
  • Impulsive means acting on sudden feelings without thinking. It captures the lack of thought but not the driving, unstoppable forward momentum of "headlong."

Think of it this way: headlong = hasty + reckless + unstoppable forward momentum, all at once.

"Headlong" works as an adverb too (he ran headlong into the wall), but as an adjective, it always sits before the noun it describes — a headlong chase, a headlong fall, a headlong rush — painting that noun with the vivid quality of wild, uncontrolled, reckless speed.
7467: Picture someone diving off a ledge — head going in first, body following behind, no way to stop, no time to think. That single image is the soul of headlong. It describes doing something at reckless speed, with your head (and the rest of you) fully committed, whether you're ready or not.
It Has Two Meanings — But They're Really One Idea

Meaning 1 — Physical (literal):
Moving with the head leading the body first. Falling, diving, or plunging in a head-first direction.

"He tripped on the stairs and fell headlong down the steps."
"She dived headlong into the pool."

Here, "headlong" is telling you how the body moved — head first, with force, with no graceful control.

Meaning 2 — Figurative (far more common):
Rushing into something with great speed but very little thought, caution, or control. Impulsively. Recklessly.

"He rushed headlong into marriage without knowing her for even a year."
"The government plunged headlong into the war."
"She fell headlong in love."

Notice what's packed into the word here: it's not just fast. It's fast and unthinking and uncontrolled — all at once. The person isn't pausing to weigh the risks. They're already in the air.
Why These Two Meanings Are the Same Idea

This is the elegant part. Think about what happens when you fall head-first:

  • Your head goes before your eyes — you can't fully see what's ahead.
  • You're moving fast, pulled by gravity or momentum.
  • You have almost no way to stop yourself mid-fall.
  • You didn't choose to land this way — it just happened, or you committed too quickly to reverse.

The figurative meaning borrows all of this. When someone rushes headlong into a decision, a relationship, or a disaster — they moved fast, they didn't look carefully, and by the time they realized what was happening, they were already deep in it.

"Headlong" is never neutral. It almost always carries a warning tone — a quiet suggestion that the speed and lack of caution might lead to trouble, or already has.

It doesn't just mean enthusiastically or eagerly. It means something closer to dangerously fast, without thinking it through, or with no safety net.

Compare:

  • "She eagerly started the new job." → Positive. Excited.
  • "She rushed headlong into the new job." → There's a shadow over it. Something might go wrong. She didn't stop to think.
More Examples to Sharpen the Meaning

"The startup charged headlong into a market they knew nothing about." (rushed in without preparation)

"He ran headlong through the crowd, knocking people aside." (physically fast, not caring about what's in the way)

"After years of caution, she finally threw herself headlong into the adventure." (fully committed, without holding back — here it's almost admiring)

"The country stumbled headlong toward a crisis." (moving toward disaster, too fast to stop)

Note that last example — "stumbled headlong." This is a common pairing: stumbled means awkwardly, without intention, and headlong adds the sense of uncontrolled speed and recklessness. Together they paint a vivid picture of someone losing their footing and tumbling forward into something bad.
How "Headlong" Is Different From Similar Words

ConceptWhat's missing compared to headlong

Hastily means quickly, but without the recklessness. You can do something hastily and still be perfectly careful.

Recklessly means without caution, but doesn't necessarily mean fast.

Impulsively means without thinking, but is softer — it doesn't carry the image of uncontrolled forward momentum.

Headlong is the only one that combines all three at once: speed + recklessness + loss of control. It's the most vivid of these because it comes with a physical picture built in.

Headlong (adverb) means:

  1. Literally — with the head going first; in a head-first direction.
  2. Figuratively (and more commonly) — at reckless, uncontrolled speed, without stopping to think or look where you're going.

The word always carries the feeling of forward momentum that is too fast and too committed to easily reverse. Whether someone is falling down a hill or rushing into a bad decision, headlong captures that moment when the body (or the mind) is already committed before wisdom had a chance to weigh in.
7468:
If someone is headstrong, it means they are strongly determined to do things their own way, and they resist being controlled, guided, or told what to do by others — even when those others might be right.

A headstrong person has their mind set on what they want, and they will push forward with it stubbornly, regardless of advice, warnings, or opposition from people around them.

Think of it this way: their "head" (their own will and thinking) is so "strong" that outside forces — other people's opinions, good advice, even common sense — simply cannot easily get through to them or steer them in another direction.
What It Really Feels Like (The Deeper Nuance)

Being headstrong is more than just being stubborn. It has two important qualities working together:

First, a refusal to be controlled or directed. A headstrong person does not want others telling them what to do. They resist authority, push back against guidance, and feel uncomfortable when someone tries to manage or influence their decisions. They want to be the one in charge of their own choices — always.

Second, an impulsive drive to act. A headstrong person doesn't just quietly disagree and sit still. They act on their own will. They move forward boldly and quickly with their own plan, often without slowing down to think things through or listen to reason. This is what separates headstrong from simply being private or quiet about your opinions.

Together, these two qualities create a person who charges ahead with their own agenda, brushes aside anyone who tries to redirect them, and can be very difficult to reason with.
How It Differs From Similar Words

This is where most learners get confused, so let's clear it up carefully.

Headstrong vs. Stubborn: A stubborn person refuses to change their position or opinion. They dig in and won't budge. A headstrong person goes a step further — they don't just refuse to change their mind, they actively push forward with their own plan, often with speed and forcefulness. Stubbornness is more passive ("I won't change"). Headstrongness is more active ("I'm doing it my way, right now, and you can't stop me").

Headstrong vs. Determined: A determined person has a strong, focused will to achieve a goal, and this is generally seen as a positive quality. Headstrong carries the same sense of strong will, but with a negative edge — it implies a reckless refusal to listen to others, even when listening would be wise. Determination is admirable. Headstrongness is concerning.

Headstrong vs. Opinionated: An opinionated person has strong views and expresses them freely. A headstrong person not only has strong views but also refuses to let anyone slow them down or change their course of action. Being opinionated is about what you say. Being headstrong is about what you do.
The Connotation: Is It Negative or Positive?

In most situations, headstrong is a negative quality. When you call someone headstrong, you are usually criticising them — suggesting that they are reckless, difficult, and unwilling to listen to wisdom or reason. A headstrong person often makes avoidable mistakes simply because they refused to slow down and take in good advice.

However, in certain contexts, headstrong can carry a faint note of reluctant admiration. If a headstrong person ends up being right — if their stubborn charge forward actually leads to success where others thought it was impossible — people might look back and say their headstrong nature was actually what made them great. Think of a young athlete who refused to listen to everyone who told her she wasn't talented enough, trained on her own terms, and became a champion. You might still call her headstrong, but with a hint of admiration in your voice.

So: headstrong is usually negative, occasionally grudgingly positive, but never purely flattering. It always implies that the person prioritises their own will over careful, open-minded thinking.

These examples will show you exactly how the word is used in real life:

"He was so headstrong that he refused to take the doctor's advice, convinced that he knew better — and ended up making his illness worse."

"The headstrong young manager never listened to her team's ideas and ended up leading the project to failure because she couldn't see past her own plans."

"Even as a child, she was headstrong — once she decided she wanted something, no one could talk her out of it."

"His headstrong nature made him a difficult employee, but you had to admire the fact that he never let anyone talk him out of what he believed in."

"The headstrong prince ignored his advisors, rode into battle without a strategy, and nearly got his entire army killed."
When Would You Actually Use This Word?

You would use headstrong when describing a person who:

  • Refuses to take advice or listen to others, especially those with more experience or knowledge.
  • Acts quickly on their own will without properly thinking through consequences.
  • Is difficult to manage, guide, or reason with — whether as a child, an employee, a leader, or a partner.
  • Pushes ahead with their plans even when there are clear signs that they should pause and reconsider.

It is commonly used to describe children who defy their parents, leaders who ignore their advisors, young people who act before they think, or anyone in a relationship or team setting who constantly overrides others and insists on their own way.

If you had to remember just one thing: a headstrong person is someone who is so fixed on their own will that they refuse to be guided, advised, or stopped by anyone else — and they act on that will boldly, often without enough thought.
7469: Think of the word head — the front of something, the leading part. Now add way, meaning a path or direction of movement. Put them together, and you get the essence of headway: moving forward from the front. Everything this word means connects back to that idea of forward movement — either physical or figurative.
Meaning 1 — Progress Toward a Goal (Most Common)

This is the meaning you will encounter the most in everyday life.

Headway means meaningful progress made toward completing something or solving something, especially when that thing is difficult or slow-going.

The word almost always appears in the phrase "make headway", which simply means to progress, to advance, or to move closer to a result.

Examples:

  • "Despite working for hours, the doctors couldn't make headway against the disease."
  • "The peace talks finally started making headway after weeks of deadlock."
  • "She's been studying hard and is slowly making headway with her maths."

Key nuance:

The word carries a feeling of effort against resistance. You don't use headway when something is easy. It quietly implies that there is something pushing back — a problem, an obstacle, a challenge — and that progress is being earned, not handed to you. This is what makes it richer than simply saying "progress."

You can also pair it with "little" or "no" to express the absence of progress:

  • "Despite all their efforts, they made little headway."
  • "Investigators made no headway in solving the case."

In its more literal sense, headway refers to the actual physical movement of something — especially a ship or boat — in a forward direction through water or space.

When a vessel is said to be "making headway," it means it is physically moving forward, as opposed to drifting, staying still, or going backward (the opposite of headway in sailing is called sternway — moving backward).

Examples:

  • "With the wind against them, the sailors struggled to make headway."
  • "The ship lost headway as it entered the calm waters of the harbour."
  • "The submarine slowly made headway through the dark depths."

This meaning also occasionally extends beyond ships — to any vehicle or object pushing forward against something (like wind or water).

This is a more technical, specialized meaning. Headway (also called headroom) refers to the vertical space or clearance between the ground (or floor) and the ceiling, arch, bridge, or structure above it.

In simple terms: it is the height of the empty space that allows people, vehicles, or objects to pass underneath something safely.

Examples:

  • "The old tunnel had very little headway, so tall trucks couldn't pass through."
  • "The bridge offers a headway of five meters above the river."
  • "Builders must ensure adequate headway on staircases for safety."

You will see this meaning in construction, engineering, architecture, and road/transport planning.
Meaning 4 — Time Gap Between Vehicles (Transport & Transit)

In public transport and traffic management, headway has a precise technical meaning: the time interval between two vehicles (buses, trains, subway cars) traveling in the same direction on the same route.

Think of it as: how long do you wait at a bus stop before the next bus comes, assuming you just missed one?

Examples:

  • "This metro line runs with a headway of 4 minutes during peak hours."
  • "Increasing the train headway to 20 minutes frustrated commuters."
  • "A shorter headway means more frequent service."

A shorter headway = vehicles come more frequently (good for passengers).
A longer headway = vehicles come less frequently (more waiting).

All four meanings share the same root logic:

MeaningWhat is moving forward?
ProgressYour work, your efforts, your goals
Nautical/vehicleA ship, boat, or vehicle
ClearanceThe space that allows forward movement
Transit intervalThe gap that controls how vehicles move forward in sequence

In every case, headway is about what stands between you and forward movement — and how much of it you are conquering.

• Headway is a neutral-to-slightly-formal word. It is perfectly natural in conversation, journalism, academic writing, and professional settings.
  • It is not slang and not overly academic — it sits comfortably in the middle.
  • Meaning 1 (progress) is used across all contexts. Meanings 3 and 4 are mostly technical and domain-specific.

If you remember nothing else, remember this:

"Make headway" = to move forward meaningfully, especially against difficulty.

Master that phrase and you have mastered the heart of this word. Everything else is a variation of the same forward-moving spirit.
